## Initial Access

| rule | severity | scope | ATT&CK | fixtures |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| **`TAD-OVER-0001`** draw a window on top of other apps | high | method | [T1660](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1660/), [T1417.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1417/002/) | 2 |
| **`TAD-OVER-0002`** request the overlay permission at runtime | medium | method | [T1660](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1660/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-OVER-0003`** phishing WebView reachable from a JavaScript bridge | medium | method | [T1660](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1660/), [T1658](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1658/) | 1 |

- **TAD-OVER-0001** — Adds a system-level overlay window. Combined with foreground-app tracking this is the classic credential-phishing primitive: a fake login drawn over the real banking app.
- **TAD-OVER-0002** — Walks the user into the "display over other apps" settings screen. Benign apps do this too (floating players, chat heads); treat it as context for the overlay capability rather than a finding on its own.
- **TAD-OVER-0003** — Loads remote content into a WebView that exposes app methods to JavaScript. Server-controlled script can then call into the app.

## Execution

| rule | severity | scope | ATT&CK | fixtures |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| **`TAD-DROP-0004`** drop a file and execute it as a process | high | class | [T1623.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1623/001/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-PERS-0003`** schedule repeated background work | low | method | [T1603](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1603/) | 1 |

- **TAD-DROP-0004** — Writes a file, marks it executable, and runs a shell or process. A native payload staged at runtime, bypassing the DEX entirely.
- **TAD-PERS-0003** — Uses JobScheduler, WorkManager or AlarmManager to get periodic execution.

| rule | severity | scope | ATT&CK | fixtures |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| **`TAD-PERS-0001`** start automatically after boot | low | apk | [T1398](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1398/), [T1624.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1624/001/) | 2 |

- **TAD-PERS-0001** — Registers a receiver for BOOT_COMPLETED. Ubiquitous in benign apps; useful as context for a payload that must survive reboots.
- **TAD-PERS-0004** — Listens for system broadcasts that provide a heartbeat — screen on/off, connectivity changes, package installs.

## Privilege Escalation

| rule | severity | scope | ATT&CK | fixtures |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| **`TAD-EXPO-0002`** shipped with android:debuggable | medium | apk | [T1404](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1404/) | 2 |

- **TAD-EXPO-0002** — The application element declares debuggable="true", so any local process that can reach the JDWP socket can attach to it, run code as the app and read its private data. A release build should never carry this; on a sample it usually means the APK was assembled quickly rather than by a release pipeline.

- **TAD-ACCS-0001** — Performs gestures, global actions or node actions from an accessibility service. This is how on-device fraud automates a real banking app: the malware, not the user, taps the buttons.
- **TAD-CRED-0003** — Aborts the SMS broadcast so the default messaging app never shows it, hiding bank alerts or stolen 2FA codes from the victim.
- **TAD-DROP-0002** — Constructs a class loader over code that is not part of the reviewed APK. Everything the loaded payload does is invisible to a scan of this file.
- **TAD-DROP-0003** — One class both decrypts data and hands it to a class loader — the shape of a packed second stage carried inside assets or raw resources.
- **TAD-DROP-0005** — Resolves classes and methods by name at runtime. Legitimate in compatibility shims, but it is also how rules that key on direct API references are dodged — treat reflection-heavy code as opaque.
- **TAD-EVAS-0001** — Compares build properties against emulator fingerprints so the payload can stay dormant in a sandbox. Also used defensively by anti-fraud SDKs.
- **TAD-EVAS-0002** — Looks for su binaries, test-keys builds or Magisk artefacts.
- **TAD-EVAS-0003** — Hunts for Frida, Xposed or ptrace attachment — the payload wants to know whether it is being hooked.
- **TAD-EVAS-0004** — Toggles a component's enabled state. Hiding the launcher alias is the malicious use; app stores and WorkManager also do it legitimately, so check which component is being disabled before drawing a conclusion.
- **TAD-EVAS-0005** — Uses device-admin powers to lock the screen, wipe, or make uninstall impossible without first revoking admin rights.
- **TAD-EVAS-0006** — Triggers removal of another package — used against security apps, and to clean up a dropper after the payload lands.
- **TAD-EVAS-0007** — Bundles a known commercial packer's runtime library. The real code is unpacked at runtime, so static coverage of this APK is limited.
- **TAD-EVAS-0008** — Reads the SIM or network country before deciding what to do. Campaigns use this to fire only in targeted countries — and to stay dormant in the analyst's.
- **TAD-EVAS-0009** — Calls Play Integrity or SafetyNet. Legitimate anti-fraud SDKs do this; so does malware that wants to know whether it is running somewhere it should stay quiet.
- **TAD-EVAS-0010** — Removes its own task from the recents list at runtime, so the user cannot see — or swipe away — what is running. (``moveTaskToBack`` alone is not enough: that is ordinary back-button handling.)
- **TAD-NAT-0001** — Calls into native code. Not suspicious by itself, but it marks the point where DEX-level analysis stops seeing what the app does.
- **TAD-PERS-0002** — Promotes a service to the foreground so Android will not kill it. Legitimate for players and trackers; also how a takeover module stays alive.

| rule | severity | scope | ATT&CK | fixtures |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| **`TAD-ACCS-0003`** track which app is in the foreground | medium | method | [T1424](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1424/), [T1418](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1418/) | 2 |
| **`TAD-COLL-0006`** enumerate installed applications | low | method | [T1418](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1418/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-COLL-0007`** collect device identifiers | low | method | [T1426](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1426/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-DISC-0001`** check whether specific packages are installed | medium | method | [T1418](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1418/), [T1424](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1424/) | 2 |

- **TAD-ACCS-0003** — Watches the foreground package, the trigger an overlay or ATS module needs in order to fire only when a targeted banking app is open.
- **TAD-COLL-0006** — Lists installed packages — reconnaissance for target selection, and for checking whether security software is present.
- **TAD-COLL-0007** — Reads IMEI / subscriber id / serial. Bot registration fingerprints, and also plain ad-tech behaviour — context matters.
- **TAD-DISC-0001** — Probes for named packages one by one rather than listing them. Overlay and ATS modules do this to decide which target app is worth attacking; so do apps checking for their own companion app, hence the repetition threshold.

- **TAD-ACCS-0002** — Harvests text from the accessibility node tree or event stream. Used to scrape balances, one-time codes and credentials out of other apps' windows without any permission held by the victim app.
- **TAD-ACCS-0004** — Observes key events from a service the user granted input access to — an accessibility service, or a custom keyboard bound as an input method.
- **TAD-COLL-0001** — Starts a MediaProjection capture or a virtual display. The remote-viewing half of a device-takeover toolkit.
- **TAD-COLL-0002** — Records audio in the background.
- **TAD-COLL-0003** — Reads contacts, typically to spread by SMS or to build target lists.
- **TAD-COLL-0004** — Reads call history.
- **TAD-COLL-0005** — Requests location updates or the last known position.
- **TAD-COLL-0008** — Reads calendar events, which leak travel, meetings and contacts.
- **TAD-COLL-0009** — Opens the camera from code. Benign in a camera app; in anything else, combined with a background trigger, it is covert capture.
- **TAD-COLL-0010** — Walks external storage and reads what it finds. Document stealers and wallet-seed hunters look exactly like this.
- **TAD-CRED-0001** — Implements a notification listener and pulls the text out of posted notifications. This is the modern OTP-theft path: no SMS permission is needed if the code arrives as a notification.
- **TAD-CRED-0002** — Parses the body of an incoming SMS. Used to lift 2FA codes, and often paired with aborting the broadcast so the user never sees the message.
- **TAD-CRED-0005** — Reads clipboard contents, where password managers, seed phrases and copied one-time codes land.
- **TAD-CRED-0006** — Answers, ends or redirects calls, or watches call state. Used to keep a victim from reaching their bank, and for call-forwarding fraud.
- **TAD-CRED-0007** — Lists the accounts registered on the device, and may ask for their auth tokens — a direct path to a signed-in service.
- **TAD-EXF-0001** — Packs data into an archive in the same class that talks to the network. Bulk exfiltration looks like this; so does crash-report upload.
- **TAD-EXPO-0001** — A provider any other app on the device can query, with no permission guarding it. Providers hand out app data — files, databases, session state — so an unprotected one is a read (and often write) primitive for anything else installed. Note that providers default to exported below targetSdk 17, which is where most of these come from.
- **TAD-EXPO-0003** — allowBackup="true" lets the app's private storage leave the device through adb backup or the cloud backup transport, without the app being involved. This is the platform default below targetSdk 31, so it is context rather than a finding — but it decides whether tokens and databases are copyable off a device someone has briefly borrowed.
- **TAD-EXPO-0004** — usesCleartextTraffic="true" re-enables plain HTTP for the whole app on targetSdk 28 and above, where the platform otherwise blocks it. Anything the app sends can then be read and rewritten by whoever runs the network. A network security config may still narrow this per domain.
- **TAD-RAT-0001** — Captures the screen in the same class that writes to the network — the remote-viewing half of a device-takeover module, as opposed to a screenshot feature that stays on the device.

## Command And Control

| rule | severity | scope | ATT&CK | fixtures |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| **`TAD-C2-0001`** Telegram Bot API used as a command channel | high | method | [T1481](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1481/), [T1437.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1437/001/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-C2-0002`** Firebase used as a command channel | medium | method | [T1481.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1481/002/), [T1437.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1437/001/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-C2-0003`** hardcoded raw-IP endpoint | medium | method | [T1437.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1437/001/), [T1509](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1509/) | 2 |
| **`TAD-C2-0004`** speak a custom protocol over a raw TCP socket | low | class | [T1509](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1509/), [T1646](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1646/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-C2-0006`** WebSocket command channel | medium | method | [T1481.002](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1481/002/), [T1437](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1437/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-C2-0007`** dead-drop resolver on a public paste or repo host | high | method | [T1481.001](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1481/001/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-DROP-0001`** install another APK through the package installer | high | method | [T1544](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1544/), [T1407](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1407/) | 2 |
| **`TAD-DROP-0006`** download an executable payload to app storage | high | class | [T1544](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1544/), [T1407](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1407/) | 1 |

- **TAD-C2-0001** — Talks to the Telegram Bot API. A free, TLS-protected, attribution-light C2 that needs no infrastructure of its own.
- **TAD-C2-0002** — Receives push messages or reads a realtime database. Common in benign apps, so weigh it together with what the handler does.
- **TAD-C2-0003** — Builds a URL against a literal IP address rather than a hostname — typical of throwaway C2 hosts, unusual in production apps.
- **TAD-C2-0004** — Opens a TCP socket and writes to it rather than going through HTTP. Remote-access modules do this for interactive control — and so does any app with its own protocol, so treat it as context, not as a finding.
- **TAD-C2-0006** — Holds a bidirectional WebSocket open. Common in chat and trading apps, and equally common as an interactive C2 for device-takeover modules.
- **TAD-C2-0007** — Fetches its real C2 address from a paste site, a raw file in a public repository or a Telegram channel — infrastructure that survives takedowns of the payload itself.
- **TAD-DROP-0001** — Drives PackageInstaller sessions or an install intent. Session-based installs are the current dropper technique of choice, because the payload never has to pass Play review.
- **TAD-DROP-0006** — Fetches a file over the network and writes it somewhere the app can load or install from — the stage between "dropper" and "second stage".

## Impact

| rule | severity | scope | ATT&CK | fixtures |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| **`TAD-CRED-0004`** send SMS without user interaction | medium | method | [T1582](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1582/) | 2 |
| **`TAD-IMP-0001`** encrypt user files in place | high | class | [T1471](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1471/) | 1 |
| **`TAD-IMP-0002`** rewrite a cryptocurrency address on the clipboard | high | class | [T1641](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1641/), [T1414](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1414/) | 2 |

- **TAD-CRED-0004** — Sends SMS from code. Used for premium-rate fraud, for spreading via the victim's contact list, and as an out-of-band C2 channel.
- **TAD-IMP-0001** — Walks files and rewrites them through a cipher. Ransomware; a backup tool that encrypts to a *new* location will not delete or overwrite the source.
- **TAD-IMP-0002** — Reads the clipboard, recognises a wallet address, and writes a different one back — the clipper pattern. Payment goes to the attacker and the user sees a plausible address.
